lines.say: This temple in southern Turkey is around eleven and a half thousand years old.
shots: q: Gobekli Tepe enclosure circle stones

lines.say: That's older than Stonehenge by six thousand years. Older than the pyramids by seven.
shots: line art: timeline 9500 BC / 3000 BC / 2560 BC

lines.say: But the strange part isn't the age. It's who built it.
shots: q: Gobekli Tepe T-shaped pillar close-up

lines.say: No pottery. No farms. No metal tools. The people who carved these five-meter pillars were hunter-gatherers.
shots: q: pillar carved boar and birds relief

lines.say: Archaeologists used to think you needed farming first, then cities, then temples.
shots: line art: arrow farming -> city -> temple

lines.say: Göbekli Tepe flipped that. The temple came first. Some researchers think feeding the builders helped push people toward farming.
shots: line art: arrows reverse, temple -> farming

lines.say: Religion may not have followed civilization. It may have started it.
shots: q: stone pillar silhouette night stars
q: torch fire light on stone texture

fact_note: c. 9500 BC (KNOWN, radiocarbon). Pre-pottery hunter-gatherer builders (KNOWN). 'Temple first, then farming' is Klaus Schmidt's interpretation (DEBATED; newer digs found domestic structures). Pillars up to ~5.5 m.
ig_caption: 11,500 years old. no farms, no pottery, no metal. hunter-gatherers carved this. the textbook order (farms, then cities, then temples) might be backwards
tt_caption: Gobekli Tepe is older than Stonehenge AND the pyramids and it was built by hunter-gatherers #gobeklitepe #ancienthistory

lines.say: In 1901, sponge divers off a Greek island pulled up a lump of corroded bronze from a Roman-era shipwreck.
shots: archive: Antikythera mechanism main fragment (Wikimedia, credit)

lines.say: For decades nobody understood it. Then X-rays and CT scans looked inside.
shots: q: x-ray scan rotating metal object

lines.say: There were gears. At least thirty of them, with triangular teeth cut by hand.
Turn a crank, and it showed where the Sun and Moon were in the sky, the Moon's phase, and when eclipses would happen, years in advance.
shots: q: Antikythera reconstruction model crank turning

lines.say: It even tracked the four-year cycle of the Olympic Games.
shots: line art: dial with four sectors

lines.say: Nothing with gearing this complex shows up again for over a thousand years, until medieval astronomical clocks.
The Greeks didn't just watch the sky. They built a machine to hold it.
shots: q: night sky over Aegean sea

fact_note: Found 1901 (KNOWN). Wreck c. 70-60 BC; device 2nd-1st c. BC (DEBATED range). ~30 surviving gears (KNOWN). Eclipses, lunar phase, Olympiad dial (KNOWN, Freeth et al. 2006/2021).
ig_caption: a crank, thirty hand-cut gears, and it predicted eclipses. pulled off a shipwreck in 1901 and nobody got it for decades
tt_caption: the Antikythera mechanism is the oldest known analog computer #antikythera #ancientgreece

lines.say: This is the Lycurgus Cup, made in Rome around sixteen hundred years ago.
shots: archive: Lycurgus Cup green, front light (Wikimedia, credit)

lines.say: Light it from the front, and it's a dull jade green.
shots: line art: arrow light from front

lines.say: Put a light inside it, and it glows blood red.
shots: archive: Lycurgus Cup red, lit from inside (Wikimedia, credit)

lines.say: For centuries nobody knew why. In 1990, scientists looked at the glass under an electron microscope.
They found particles of gold and silver, about fifty to a hundred nanometers wide, a thousand times thinner than a hair.
shots: line art: hair vs nanoparticle scale

lines.say: Those particles scatter light one way and let it through another. Today we call that nanotechnology.
shots: line art: light wave hitting particles, splitting green / red

lines.say: The Romans almost certainly didn't understand it. But they made it work, probably by accident, and kept the recipe.

fact_note: Lycurgus Cup, 4th c. AD Roman (KNOWN). Dichroic: green reflected, red transmitted (KNOWN). Gold-silver nanoparticles ~50-100 nm, TEM study Barber & Freestone 1990 (KNOWN). Whether deliberate is DEBATED. Cup is in the British Museum: use Wikimedia photos ONLY if licence allows commercial use and not BM-owned images; else redraw.
ig_caption: same cup, same glass. green from the outside, red when lit from inside. romans pulled off nanotech by accident
tt_caption: the Lycurgus Cup, Roman nanotechnology from 1600 years ago #romanempire #ancienttech

lines.say: You've probably seen it. The Baghdad Battery, proof that ancient people had electricity.
shots: q: clay jar replica copper cylinder

lines.say: Here's what it actually is. A clay jar, a copper cylinder, an iron rod. Found near Baghdad and described in 1938.
shots: line art: cross-section jar, copper, iron rod labeled

lines.say: Fill it with vinegar, and yes, you get about half a volt. People have tested it.
But nothing else fits. No wires were ever found. No other battery parts. Nothing it could have powered.
And the iron rod was sealed inside with asphalt, which makes it hard to connect to anything.
shots: line art: seal on top of jar

lines.say: Most archaeologists think it held rolled scrolls, like similar jars from the region, and the metal simply corroded.
It can make electricity. There's just no sign anyone ever used it that way.
shots: q: clay jar silhouette dark background
q: dust particles in light beam

fact_note: Described by Wilhelm Koenig 1938 (KNOWN). Parthian or Sasanian date (DEBATED). Replicas give ~0.5-2 V (KNOWN). Scroll-storage interpretation (DEBATED, mainstream). No conductors found (KNOWN).
ig_caption: I used to believe the Baghdad battery thing. turns out it can make half a volt with vinegar... and that's about all we can say for sure
tt_caption: Baghdad battery: what the evidence actually shows #ancientmysteries #mythbusting

lines.say: In 612 BC, the city of Nineveh was sacked and burned.
shots: archive: 19th c. engraving fall of Nineveh (public domain)
q: fire flames dark slow motion

lines.say: Inside the palace was the library of King Ashurbanipal. Tens of thousands of clay tablets.
Paper burns. Parchment burns. But clay does something else in a fire. It bakes.
The blaze that destroyed the city hardened the tablets and kept them under the rubble for two and a half thousand years.
In the 1850s they were dug up and shipped to London. Among them was the Epic of Gilgamesh.
In 1872, a young scholar named George Smith read one tablet and found a flood story: a boat, and birds sent out to find land.
shots: line art: boat on waves, dove

lines.say: Burning the library is the reason we can still read it.

fact_note: Nineveh fell 612 BC (KNOWN). ~30,000 tablets/fragments (KNOWN). Fire-hardening helped preservation (KNOWN, commonly stated). Layard/Rassam excavations 1849-1850s (KNOWN). George Smith 1872 (KNOWN). Ties to ep. 1 (Utnapishtim) without repeating it. No BM photos.
ig_caption: the fire that burned Nineveh basically baked its library into stone. that's why we can read Gilgamesh today
tt_caption: how a fire preserved the Library of Ashurbanipal #gilgamesh #ancienthistory

lines.say: Sixty seconds, sixty minutes. Why sixty, when we count everything else in tens?
Blame Mesopotamia. Over four thousand years ago, Sumerian and later Babylonian scribes counted in base sixty.
Sixty is great for trade. It divides cleanly by two, three, four, five, six, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty and thirty.
shots: line art: 60 splitting into equal slices

lines.say: Babylonian astronomers used it to track the sky. Greek astronomers like Ptolemy copied their system.
So when the hour was later cut into smaller pieces, it was cut the Babylonian way.
shots: line art: hour circle divided into 60

lines.say: Same with the circle. Three hundred and sixty degrees. Six times sixty.
shots: line art: circle with 360 degree marks, phi overlay

lines.say: Every time you check the time, you're using math invented by people who wrote on clay.

fact_note: Sexagesimal from Sumer, developed by Babylonians (KNOWN). Greek astronomers used sexagesimal fractions (KNOWN). Hour subdivision into 60 came later through astronomy (KNOWN). 360 degrees tied to Babylonian astronomy (KNOWN; exact origin DEBATED).
ig_caption: never thought about why an hour is 60 minutes until today. it's Babylonian math. we're still counting like it's 2000 BC

hook: The diary of a man who|built the *Great Pyramid*

lines.say: In 2013, on Egypt's Red Sea coast, archaeologists found the oldest inscribed papyri ever discovered.
shots: q: Red Sea coast Egypt desert aerial

lines.say: They were the logbook of an official named Merer, written about forty-five hundred years ago.
shots: line art: hieratic script on papyrus

lines.say: Merer ran a crew of about forty men. Their job: carry limestone by boat from the quarries at Tura, along the Nile, to Giza.
shots: line art: map Tura -> Giza along Nile

lines.say: For King Khufu. The pyramid we call the Great Pyramid.
shots: q: Great Pyramid of Giza low angle

lines.say: He writes it like a work schedule. Loaded stones. Sailed. Spent the night. Sailed again.
No aliens. No lost technology. A shipping crew, a canal, and a guy keeping careful notes.
shots: q: pyramid casing limestone blocks close

lines.say: And somehow that's more impressive.

fact_note: Wadi al-Jarf papyri, found 2013 by Pierre Tallet (KNOWN). Merer's diary, Khufu's reign c. 2560 BC (KNOWN). ~40-man crew, Tura limestone to Giza (KNOWN). Oldest inscribed papyri known (KNOWN).
ig_caption: the guy who shipped limestone for the Great Pyramid kept a work diary. we found it in 2013. it reads like a delivery log
tt_caption: Diary of Merer, the oldest papyrus ever found, is about building the Great Pyramid #egypt #pyramids

lines.say: This is a clay tablet called Plimpton 322. It's about thirty-eight hundred years old.
shots: line art: Plimpton 322 grid redraw, slow push

lines.say: It's a table. Four columns, fifteen rows, numbers in base sixty.
shots: line art: columns highlight one by one

lines.say: In 1945, scholars worked out what the numbers were. Sets of whole numbers that make right triangles.
shots: line art: right triangle sides labeled
q: old library books desk lamp

lines.say: Like three, four, five. Except these get huge. One row has twelve thousand seven hundred and nine, and eighteen thousand five hundred and forty-one.
That's the Pythagorean theorem at work, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born.
What it was for is still argued. A teacher's list of problems, or something like a trigonometry table.
shots: line art: question mark over tablet

lines.say: Either way, someone in Babylon knew this rule very well.

fact_note: Plimpton 322, Columbia University, c. 1800 BC (KNOWN). Triples identified by Neugebauer & Sachs 1945 (KNOWN). 12709/18541 is row 4 (KNOWN). Purpose DEBATED (Robson; Mansfield & Wildberger 2017). Use redraw unless free licence confirmed.
ig_caption: a Babylonian tablet full of Pythagorean triples. a thousand years before Pythagoras. what it was FOR is still a fight
tt_caption: Plimpton 322 shows Babylonians knew the Pythagorean theorem #math #babylon

lines.say: Modern concrete cracks within decades. Roman harbors have stood in seawater for two thousand years.
For a long time the answer was volcanic ash. That's part of it.
But in 2023, an MIT team found something else. Tiny white chunks of lime scattered through the concrete.
shots: line art: circles around white clasts

lines.say: Everyone assumed those were mistakes, bad mixing. They weren't.
The Romans likely mixed in hot quicklime. When a crack forms and water gets in, those lime chunks dissolve and refill the crack with fresh mineral.
shots: line art: crack forms, water enters, crack seals

lines.say: The team made their own version, cracked it, ran water through, and in two weeks the cracks had sealed.
shots: line art: day 0 -> day 14 crack closing

lines.say: The Pantheon's dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth.

fact_note: Seger, Masic et al., Science Advances, Jan 2023 (KNOWN): hot mixing, lime clasts self-heal; samples sealed in ~2 weeks. Pozzolanic ash (KNOWN). Pantheon largest unreinforced concrete dome (KNOWN).
ig_caption: the 'mistakes' in Roman concrete were actually the reason it lasts 2000 years. little lime chunks that patch cracks when water gets in
tt_caption: why Roman concrete lasts thousands of years #romanempire #engineering

lines.say: Three things you used today that started in ancient Mesopotamia.
One. Writing. Around 3200 BC in Uruk, scribes pressed reeds into clay to track grain and beer. The first written words were basically receipts.
Two. The wheel. Some of the earliest known wheels appear in Mesopotamia around then, first for pottery, then for carts.
Three. The week. Mesopotamian astronomers gave special weight to seven, the seven lights that wander across the sky: the Sun, the Moon, and five planets.
shots: line art: seven circles in a row

lines.say: Those seven still sit inside the names of our days. Sunday. Monday. Saturday, for Saturn.
shots: line art: weekday names with planet symbols

lines.say: Writing, wheels, weeks. Five thousand years old, and still running your life.

fact_note: Proto-cuneiform at Uruk c. 3200 BC, administrative (KNOWN). Wheel: Mesopotamia c. 3500 BC among earliest, Ljubljana wheel comparably old (DEBATED origin; wording 'some of the earliest'). Seven-day week via Babylonian sevens and Hellenistic planet-days (KNOWN chain, exact origin DEBATED).
ig_caption: writing started as beer receipts. not even joking
tt_caption: 3 Sumerian inventions you still use every day #sumer #history
